artist.artist_description: Michael Jackson, an American musician, was born in Gary, Indiana, and rose to fame as the lead singer of the Jackson 5. Known as the "King of Pop," he revolutionized the music industry with his innovative dance moves, including the moonwalk, and albums like "Thriller," which remains the best-selling album of all time. His influence extended beyond music into fashion and dance, making him a global cultural icon.

Madonna, an American singer, songwriter, and actress, was born in Bay City, Michigan, and rose to fame in the early 1980s with her unique blend of pop and dance music. Known as the "Queen of Pop," she has achieved numerous milestones, including over 300 million records sold worldwide and a record 38 top-ten singles on the Billboard Hot 100. Beyond her music, Madonna is celebrated for her cultural impact, pushing boundaries with her provocative performances and advocacy for social issues like AIDS awareness and gay rights.

The Police, a British rock band formed in 1977, consists of Sting (lead vocals, bass), Stewart Copeland (drums), and Andy Summers (guitar). Originating from London, they gained fame with their unique blend of rock, reggae, and jazz, achieving worldwide success with hits like "Roxanne" and "Every Breath You Take." Sting, formerly a schoolteacher, brought a thoughtful lyricism to the band, which earned them five Grammy Awards and induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2003.

Guns N' Roses is an American hard rock band formed in Los Angeles in 1985, known for their raw energy and rebellious attitude. The band's classic lineup, featuring Axl Rose and Slash, achieved massive success with albums like "Appetite for Destruction," which became the best-selling debut album ever. Their tumultuous history and iconic hits like "Sweet Child O' Mine" have cemented their status as rock legends, while their influence extends into fashion and popular culture.

a-ha is a Norwegian synth-pop band formed in 1982, known for their iconic hit "Take On Me." The band, consisting of Morten Harket, Magne Furuholmen, and Pål Waaktaar-Savoy, gained international fame with their innovative music videos and catchy melodies. They have sold over 100 million records worldwide and continue to be celebrated for their contributions to pop music.

U2, an Irish rock band formed in 1976, consists of Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr., who met as teenagers in Dublin. They gained international fame with their album "The Joshua Tree" in 1987, which included hits like "With or Without You" and "I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For." Known for their politically and socially conscious lyrics, U2 has won 22 Grammy Awards and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005.

Joan Jett & the Blackhearts is an American rock band formed in 1980, led by Joan Jett, who was born Joan Marie Larkin in Wynnewood, Pennsylvania. Jett gained fame as the guitarist and co-founder of the all-female rock band The Runaways before launching her solo career. The band is best known for their hit "I Love Rock 'n' Roll," and Jett's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2015 highlights her significant impact on rock music.

Cyndi Lauper, an American singer, songwriter, and actress, rose to fame in the 1980s with her vibrant pop music and distinctive voice. Born in Astoria, New York, she overcame early struggles in the music industry to achieve success with hits like "Girls Just Want to Have Fun" and "Time After Time." Lauper is also known for her advocacy for LGBTQ rights and her Tony Award-winning work on the Broadway musical "Kinky Boots."

Culture Club is a British pop band formed in 1981, known for their unique blend of pop, rock, and new wave music. The band, fronted by the charismatic Boy George, rose to fame with hits like "Karma Chameleon" and "Do You Really Want to Hurt Me," earning them a BRIT Award for Best British Group in 1983. Boy George's androgynous style and the band's embrace of diverse cultural influences made them icons of the 1980s, challenging societal norms around gender and sexuality.

Simple Minds, a Scottish rock band formed in Glasgow in 1977, are known for their new wave and pop rock sound. They achieved international success with hits like "Don't You (Forget About Me)" from the movie "The Breakfast Club." Frontman Jim Kerr's marriage to Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders added to their cultural footprint in the music world.

Soft Cell is a British synth-pop duo formed in 1980 by Marc Almond and David Ball in Sheffield, England. They achieved international fame with their hit single "Tainted Love," which became one of the best-selling singles of all time in the UK. Marc Almond's distinctive voice and the band's provocative lyrics, often exploring themes of love and sexuality, cemented their place in the New Romantic movement of the early 1980s.

Survivor is an American rock band formed in Chicago in 1978, known for their arena rock style. They achieved fame with hits like "Eye of the Tiger," which won a Grammy and was featured in the movie Rocky III. The band's name reflects their determination to succeed, and they continue to be celebrated for their contributions to rock music.

Bon Jovi, an American rock band formed in 1983 in Sayreville, New Jersey, was founded by lead singer Jon Bon Jovi. They gained fame with their third album, "Slippery When Wet," which included hits like "Livin' on a Prayer" and "You Give Love a Bad Name." The band has sold over 130 million records worldwide and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.

Def Leppard is a British rock band formed in Sheffield, England, in 1977, known for their hard rock and heavy metal sound. They achieved massive success with albums like "Pyromania" and "Hysteria," the latter featuring hits like "Pour Some Sugar on Me." Notably, drummer Rick Allen continued to perform after losing an arm in a car accident, showcasing the band's resilience and dedication to their music.

Eurythmics, a British pop duo formed in 1980 by Annie Lennox and Dave Stewart, rose to fame with their innovative blend of new wave, pop, and rock music. Originally from Aberdeen, Scotland, and Sunderland, England respectively, Lennox and Stewart met in London and quickly became known for hits like "Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)" and "Here Comes the Rain Again." They won the Best British Group at the Brit Awards in 1984 and were inducted into the UK Music Hall of Fame in 2005, leaving a lasting impact on music and fashion with Lennox's androgynous style.

Pet Shop Boys, a British synth-pop duo formed in 1981 by Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe, rose to fame with hits like "West End Girls" and "It's a Sin." Tennant, a former journalist, met Lowe in a hi-fi shop, sparking their musical collaboration. They've sold over 50 million records, won numerous awards, and are known for their sophisticated pop sound and witty lyrics, often addressing social and political themes.

Poison is an American rock band formed in 1983 in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, known for their glam metal style. The band, fronted by Bret Michaels, achieved significant success in the late 1980s and early 1990s with hits like "Every Rose Has Its Thorn" and "Nothin' but a Good Time." Interestingly, Bret Michaels has also competed on reality TV shows, including winning "The Masked Singer" in 2020.

George Michael, a British singer-songwriter, rose to fame as part of the duo Wham! in the early 1980s before embarking on a successful solo career. Known for his soulful voice and hits like "Careless Whisper" and "Faith," he sold over 100 million records worldwide. Michael was openly gay and used his platform to advocate for AIDS awareness and gay rights, leaving a lasting impact on both music and culture.

INXS is an Australian rock band formed in Sydney in 1977, known for their fusion of rock, new wave, and funk. The band achieved international success with hits like "Need You Tonight" and "Never Tear Us Apart," and sold over 75 million records worldwide. Lead singer Michael Hutchence's charismatic stage presence and tragic death in 1997 added a poignant chapter to the band's storied history.

track.detail: This track, released in 1983, not only topped the charts but also revolutionized music videos with its iconic moonwalk. It was part of the 'Thriller' album, which remains the best-selling album of all time. The song's bassline, inspired by Hall & Oates, became instantly recognizable, and its narrative about paternity rumors added a layer of intrigue. Its impact extended beyond music, influencing fashion with the single white glove and sparking discussions on race and celebrity in the media.

Released in 1984, this song catapulted its singer to superstardom, becoming a symbol of sexual liberation and empowerment. The music video, featuring the singer in a gondola in Venice, became a cultural phenomenon. It was controversial yet embraced, sparking debates on feminism and media portrayal of women. The track's success helped solidify MTV's influence on pop culture, and its singer's bold fashion choices set trends that are still referenced today.

This 1983 release, often misinterpreted as a love song, is actually about obsessive surveillance. It became a massive hit, topping charts worldwide and winning two Grammy Awards. The song's minimalist arrangement, featuring a simple yet effective bassline and Sting's emotive vocals, made it timeless. Its influence spread to various genres, and it has been covered by numerous artists, cementing its place in music history.

Originally a playful riff by Slash, this 1987 track became an anthem of the era. Its soaring guitar solo and heartfelt lyrics about love and longing resonated with listeners. The song's success propelled its band to international fame, and its video, featuring the band in a warehouse, captured the raw energy of rock. It remains a staple at weddings and sporting events, symbolizing the enduring appeal of rock music.

This 1985 hit is renowned for its groundbreaking music video, which combined live-action with pencil-sketch animation. The song's distinctive synth riff and falsetto vocals became iconic. It topped charts globally and won multiple awards, including six MTV Video Music Awards. The track's success helped popularize synth-pop and influenced the visual style of music videos in the following decades.

Released in 1987, this track became a defining moment for its band, blending rock with introspective lyrics. The song's minimalist arrangement, featuring a haunting guitar riff and Bono's passionate vocals, struck a chord with listeners. It topped charts and won a Grammy for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal. Its impact extended to live performances, where it became a staple, often accompanied by powerful visuals and audience participation.

Originally released in 1981, this cover of an Arrows song became an anthem of female empowerment in rock music. Its catchy riff and rebellious lyrics resonated with a generation. The track's success helped break down gender barriers in the music industry, and its singer's leather-clad image became iconic. It remains a staple at parties and sporting events, symbolizing the enduring spirit of rock 'n' roll.

track.track_display_name: Girls Just Want to Have Fun
track.detail: Released in 1983, this song became an anthem of female empowerment and joy. Its colorful music video, featuring a diverse group of women, broke stereotypes and celebrated individuality. The track's success helped its singer become a pop icon, known for her distinctive voice and eclectic style. It remains a beloved party song, symbolizing the carefree spirit of the era.

This 1983 release, co-written with Rob Hyman, showcased its singer's versatility and emotional depth. The song's simple yet powerful lyrics about love and loss resonated with listeners. It became a chart-topping hit and won a Grammy for Best New Artist. The track's success helped solidify its singer's place in music history, and its timeless appeal has led to numerous covers and uses in film and television.

Released in 1983, this track became a global phenomenon, topping charts and winning a Brit Award for Best Single. Its catchy melody and lyrics about identity and acceptance struck a chord with listeners. The song's success helped popularize androgynous fashion and multiculturalism in music. Its music video, featuring vibrant colors and diverse characters, became iconic, symbolizing the era's embrace of diversity and self-expression.

This iconic track was famously featured in the closing scene of the classic teen movie 'The Breakfast Club,' where its emotional resonance perfectly captured the film's theme of unity among diverse high school students. Released in 1985, it not only became a symbol of the era but also a timeless piece that continues to evoke nostalgia. Interestingly, the band initially resisted recording the song, feeling it didn't fit their style, yet it became their biggest hit, showcasing the unpredictable nature of music's impact.

Originally a 1965 Northern Soul hit, this cover version transformed the song into a synth-pop masterpiece upon its release in 1981. It became the best-selling single in the UK that year and held the record for the longest consecutive weeks at number one for a British act. The song's haunting melody and Marc Almond's distinctive vocals made it a staple in clubs and a symbol of the burgeoning electronic music scene, influencing countless artists in the decades to follow.

This track was specifically written for the movie 'Rocky III' in 1982, where it perfectly encapsulated the film's theme of perseverance and triumph. It not only won a Grammy for Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal but also became a cultural phenomenon, inspiring countless athletes and fitness enthusiasts. The song's driving beat and motivational lyrics have made it a timeless classic that continues to energize listeners around the world.

Released in 1986, this song became an anthem for the working class, resonating with its story of Tommy and Gina's struggles and dreams. It not only topped the charts in the U.S. but also became a global hit, showcasing the universal appeal of its message. The song's iconic opening riff and Jon Bon Jovi's passionate vocals have made it a staple at sporting events and a symbol of resilience and hope.

Originally intended as a filler track for their 1987 album 'Hysteria,' this song unexpectedly became one of the band's biggest hits. Its infectious guitar riff and suggestive lyrics made it a favorite in strip clubs, which helped propel it to mainstream success. The song's enduring popularity is a testament to its catchy melody and the band's ability to create music that resonates across generations.

Released in 1983, this track's innovative use of synthesizers and Annie Lennox's androgynous image broke new ground in music and fashion. The song's cryptic lyrics and mesmerizing beat made it an instant classic, influencing a wide range of artists and genres. It remains a powerful example of how music can transcend boundaries and inspire creativity.

This track, released in 1984, combined elements of hip-hop, synth-pop, and social commentary, making it a unique and influential hit. Its lyrics, inspired by T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land,' offered a critique of class and culture that resonated with listeners. The song's success marked the beginning of a new era in pop music, where artistry and social awareness could coexist on the charts.

Written in a laundromat in 1988, this song's raw emotion and relatable lyrics about love and heartbreak struck a chord with audiences. It became the band's only number one hit and a staple of '80s rock, showcasing the power of vulnerability in music. The song's acoustic guitar intro and Bret Michaels' heartfelt vocals have made it a timeless classic that continues to resonate with listeners.

Released in 1987, this track marked George Michael's successful transition from a teen idol to a mature artist. Its funky bassline and catchy chorus made it an instant hit, while its music video, featuring Michael's iconic leather jacket and jukebox dance, became a cultural phenomenon. The song's message of self-assurance and its infectious groove have made it a timeless anthem of personal empowerment.

Released in 1987, this track's minimalist production and Michael Hutchence's seductive vocals made it an instant classic. It became the band's only number one hit in the U.S. and showcased their ability to blend rock and dance music seamlessly. The song's iconic music video, featuring Hutchence's intense performance, further cemented its place in pop culture, making it a symbol of the era's sensuality and style.
